63	
64	## The standing goal
65	
66	You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.
67	
68	- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
69	- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
70	- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
71	
72	## The curator's role and decisions
73	
74	The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
75	
76	Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
77	
78	A decision is consequential if it:
79	
80	- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
81	- touches microGPT: a line of the model program, its speed or its readability;
82	- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
83	- or cannot be undone.
84	
85	It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
86	
87	1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
88	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
89	3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
90	
91	Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
92	
93	- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
94	- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
95	- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
96	- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
97	- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
98	- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
99	- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
100	- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
101	- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
102	- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.
103	
104	## The facts of this environment
105	
106	- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
107	- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
108	- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
109	- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
110	- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
111	- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
112	- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
113	- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
114	- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
115	- The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn. Its reminders are advisory.
116	- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
117	- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
118	- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.
119	
120	## Talking to the curator
121	
122	- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
123	- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
124	- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
125	- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
126	- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
127	- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
128	- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
129	- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
130	- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
131	- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
132	- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
133	- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.
134	
135	**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:
136	
137	1. The question, in one line.
138	2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
139	3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
140	4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
141	5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
142	
143	Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
144	
145	Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
146	
147	**Quiet times.**
148	
149	- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
150	- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone, or after a process stop the hook's one line.
151	- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
152	- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end or a hold. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
153	
154	**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. Your default, an answer to each point as it comes, buries the curator in text.
155	
156	- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
157	- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
158	- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing.
159	- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
160	
161	**Pages.**
162	
163	- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
164	- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
165	- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
166	- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
167	- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
168	- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
169	
170	## The record: what goes where
171	
172	Under `explorations/coordinator/`:
173	
174	- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
175	- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
176	- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
177	- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
178	- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
179	- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
180	- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages.
181	- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
182	- `review-queue.md`: the review lists, sorted by theme.
183	
184	Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.
185	
186	FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.
187	
188	- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
189	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
190	- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
191	- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
192	- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.
193	
194	## The boot
195	
196	At session start and after each compaction, read these in order:
197	
198	1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
199	2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
200	3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
201	4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
202	5. The boot note, then the held list.
203	6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
204	7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
205	
206	- Read nothing else. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
207	- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
208	- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
209	- After each process stop, tell the curator in one line that the git-check hook is back on. Only the curator can turn it off again, by switching the session to manual mode (`cloud-container`, its hooks part).
210	
211	## The parts
212	
213	- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
214	- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
215	- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
216	- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`.
217	- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
218	- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
219	- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.

5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone, or after a process stop the hook's one line.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end or a hold. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. Your default, an answer to each point as it comes, buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages.
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review lists, sorted by theme.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.

- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, read these in order:

1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.

6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). It exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, when the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed commits. When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

To turn the hook off, give the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0. Keep the original in the session's scratchpad:

    cp ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh <scratchpad>/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig
    printf '#!/bin/bash\ncat >/dev/null\nexit 0\n' > ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh

- The automatic permission check refuses this step in auto mode, and also a check-in whose prompt would take it. The step runs only after the curator switches the session to manual approval, where each tool call waits for the curator.
- In manual approval, every command of a Workflow agent also waits for the curator's approval. So a batch runs unattended only in auto mode: after the step, ask the curator to switch back.
- Every start of the process writes the original script again. So after each process stop the hook is back on: `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` prints 1 or more. The `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The boot", says how the curator is told.

# The transcript backup and the git-check hook

This part is for the coordinating session. Two Stop hooks run in this container.

## The transcript backup

The backup's Stop hook runs `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh`. The hook returns at once, and a detached runner does the work. It copies the transcripts of every session in the container, Workflow agents' included, into that worktree of the orphan branch `transcripts-blinded`. Then it commits, pushes and packs. A pass takes about 10 s and writes one line to the worktree's `.backup.log`, which keeps the last 200.

The tracked `.claude/settings.json` registers the hook, beside the compaction hook. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` adds it to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if the tracked file does not. If both files register it, each turn's end runs two passes, about 4 s apart, which the backup's lock runs one after the other. They do no harm.

Its blind spots:

- It runs when a turn of the main session ends, not when an agent finishes. A session inside one long turn is not backed up, however much its agents do. Check-ins end turns (`stops.md`).
- It copies transcripts, not trees. Uncommitted work in a worktree is not covered.
- If the container dies within about 10 s of a turn's end, that turn's snapshot is lost.
- It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push is silent. At each check-in and after each process stop, read the log's last line, or the branch's state. A good pass reads `push=ok`, or `ahead=0 push=none`.

      tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log
      git -C /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded status -sb

- The runner removes only an `index.lock` that is at least 10 s old and that no process holds open. A stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed` in the log). If no process holds it open, remove it by hand.

The scripts that run are the copies in the worktree's `scripts/`. The reference copies in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` change nothing until you copy them into the worktree. If a pass fails in a way that this section does not name, print `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md#Three traps'`, and the same for "How the snapshot works".

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

To turn the hook off, give the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0. Keep the original in the session's scratchpad:

# The platform's stops, and check-ins

This part says when the platform's stops come, how to tell them apart, and what they do here. What any process stop kills and keeps, and a worker's steps after one, are `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. How to resume a run is the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

## What stops the process

- **The cap.** The platform stops the process after about 12 h 58 min of continuous running, and starts it again in resume mode, the same session, within seconds. No crash, memory limit or message causes it. The next stop comes 12 h 58 min after the last start.
- **Idleness.** The process also ends when the session goes idle, after a few minutes to a few hours. It runs continuously only while the curator or a check-in keeps it busy, so the cap's stops fall in busy stretches.
- **A VM restart.** The machine boots again. The disk usually survives (below).

Every start, after a VM restart too, resets the cap's clock.

The environment manager's log records every stop and start:

    grep -E 'Received signal|context cancellation|Set session mode' /tmp/env-manager.log | tail

A stop is three lines: a `SIGTERM` ("Received signal, shutting down gracefully"), then "Claude Code stopped due to context cancellation" with the run's length in `duration_ms`, then "Set session mode for environment" `resume`, the next start. To tell the kinds apart:

- The cap's stop has a `duration_ms` near 46,640,000.
- An idle stop has a shorter one, and the boot time that `uptime -s` prints stays earlier than the stop.
- After a VM restart, `uptime -s` prints a boot time between the stop and the next start.

## A VM restart that rolls the disk back

A VM restart can bring the disk back to an earlier state. Other restarts have kept it whole, and nothing tells in advance which kind comes. So only what is pushed is safe.

The signs of a rollback:

- The local `main` ends at an earlier commit, and the commits made since are on `origin` only. The reflog jumps from that commit to the first commit made after the restart.
- The newer files of the scratchpad and of the tree's `tmp/` are gone, and so are the later lines of the backup's log. The session's own transcript stays whole.

To recover:

1. Run `git fetch`.
2. On each branch that you work on, `main` included, run `git rebase origin/<branch>`. With no commit after the restart, this moves the branch forward to the pushed commit.
3. Push your own commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says.
4. In the coordinating session, after the next turn ends, read the backup's last log line (`hooks.md`).

If the source file of a published Artifact page was lost, the `coordinator` skill says how to rebuild it from the page.

## The weekly usage limit

When the account's weekly limit on all models is reached, each new agent launch is refused ("You've hit your weekly limit"), and a running Workflow run ends. Later, turns and launches can be served again while the usage panel still shows the limit as reached. A launch that succeeds is the sign. If the limit ended a run, resume it as after a process stop.

## What a stop kills and keeps here

Any process stop kills and keeps what `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md` says. On this platform, also:

- `send_later` reminders survive. They live on the server.
- A command started with `nohup` survives the cap and an idle stop. A VM restart ends every process.
- The git-check hook is back on (`hooks.md`).

A new session is not a process stop. It starts on a fresh machine and cannot resume another session's run. Only its pushed work and the files of the repository carry over.

## Check-ins, for the coordinating session

Check-ins keep the session busy across a long run. Each wake falls inside the main session's one-hour prompt cache, so it reads the cache instead of writing the whole context again. Each turn's end also runs the transcript backup (`hooks.md`).

- Arm all the check-ins of a series in one turn, 45 minutes apart. Use no cron trigger, whose shortest interval is an hour. Do not chain reminders, each check-in arming the next one.

## C. What the reviewers missed

Only what is consequential and that none of the three named.

1. **Row 774, walk's half of conditional extension, is a batch-19 candidate that carries question 2 into walk's values under the standing go.** PLAN phase 3, item 17 lists "walk's half of conditional extension (row 774), which changes walk's values, since a list of tuples or of floats loses its `<`". Part 2, 25 judged question 2 and part 2, 29 named row 774 as what batch 18 caused, but neither said that the next batch would land the departure in walk at its default, with no word of his. It is held out of batch 19 until he answers question 2 (section A, part 2, 25).
2. **The conflict between "the checker at a true zero" and P-85 is a defect of the plan's text, not an act of the window.** Part 3, 18c named the conflict as what the reorientation hid; none of the parts said that PLAN's phase 3 has carried it since the consolidation of 2026-10-15 ("Not candidates: the arrays' 21 sites ... (item 13)"), so the ask is owed whatever the window did (section A, part 3, 18c).
3. **The record leaned on a held line as his approval.** `CLIMB-BATCH-17.md:69` supports item 56's default with "Your held note of 19:53 UTC on 2026-10-16 read the 42, this variant's figure, as plainly good news to keep", and Fable's review of the record let it stand. `HELD.md`'s header says being on the list answers nothing. The line is cut in the fix of `CLIMB-BATCH-17.md` (section D.1), and the rule goes to the skill writer with the 19:57 rule: a held line is never cited as the curator's yes.
4. **The P-152 probe can start now and was deferred three times** (batch 17's record, batch 18's scope, "Nothing else starts before the review" in `BOOT.md:10`). It needs no go and no answer of his (section A, part 1, E21). It is in the Opus work below.
5. **The two unlanded shadows are the only probe state a lost container would cost**, `-opsort` and `-strings` (section A, part 3, 9); the parts counted branches and worktrees but did not say which held work not on `main`.

I made all three parts as three commits on `main`. The lint is clean on every changed file, and nothing is pushed.

## Commits

**A. `c3e2b8e1f`, `fortress-repo`.** `revival-changes.md` grew from 54,927 to 59,256 bytes.
- **Conditional extension:** a new entry under "Static parameters", next to the other `where` entries (I chose the place).
  - Its rule follows FACTS F-255 as the repair corrected it. The constraints hold while the checker checks the entry itself, the value parameters and the members.
  - They do not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters and own `where` clause, the `throws` clause and contract, or the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses.
  - It also gives the `List` change, and rows 773 and 774 as departures.
  - I checked the rule against `TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:190-236` and `List.fsi:67-68`.
- **`:46`:**
  - It now says "every pair of functions, one at least generic".
  - A new sentence: "A functional method of a generic trait or object is still compared on the instance that a call makes."
  - Each refusal is a list item with its message: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" and "fails the Meet Rule".
  - A pair that walk does not read this way keeps the team's message.
  - "four cases" became "six cases", with rows 779 and 780 added.
- **`:148`:**
  - "Where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other, it compares such a method with another of the set on those domains. Elsewhere it compares them on the instance that the call makes."
  - The sentence on row 766 is replaced. A trait's generic method now reads its bounds and coercions as an object's does, with the `Box[\ZZ64\]` example.
  - One added sentence keeps the error left by F-253: a call with an argument outside a bound still fails with an error of unification that reads no bound.
- **`:189-193`:**
  - The constraint is now checked in three places: at a call, at a dotted call, and at a type's use (constructor calls included).
  - A `where`-clause variable is inferred at the call.
  - Two cases are not built: a bound that names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable, and row 470.
  - Walk's row 777 is named, and the reason cites the where calculus.
- **`:217`:** "That type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints on the variable. A bound that names the variable, such as `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, names that type." A new sentence says the checker reads an extender against the listed type at the same types.
- **`:220`:** "walk reads the extenders at every type of a bounded variable (ledger row 754), and reads the variable for the same name in another declaration's bound (ledger row 778);"
- **`:222`:** "the code generator does not compile a trait with a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 701)."
- **`compiler.md:39`:** "It also refuses a function, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. A trait's or object's contract never reaches it: the disambiguator drops it (ledger row 781)." I checked this against the guards at `CodeGen.java:2967`, `:4107` and `:5027`.
- **`interpreter.md:38`:** "It reads every pair of functions, one at least generic, on their declared domains, each over its own instances. It compares a functional method of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes."
- **`sources.md`:** a new section, "Climb batch 18's changes, 2026-10-19", with six lines.

**B. `fd0cf67dd`, hooks.**
- **`hooks.md`** went from 4,013 to 3,719 bytes.
  - The step by hand and the two bullets on manual approval are gone.
  - In their place: the switch runs at every SessionStart and Stop, gives the script its empty body, and keeps the launcher's script as `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`.
  - The `grep -c stop_hook_active` test stays.
  - A new bullet says the switch can miss one turn, which is answered as before.
- **`stops.md:51`:** "The launcher writes the git-check hook again, and the git-check switch turns it off at the start (`hooks.md`)."
- **`coordinator` `SKILL.md`, "The boot":**
  - The lead now says "take these steps in order".
  - Step 0 checks the model with `get_session` and the two fields.
  - The git-check line at `:209` is replaced by the model-check line: the alarm comes at every turn on neither Opus nor Fable, and the session makes it the first line, pushes it, and does no other work.
- `:151` stays as it was.
- Both skills' `sources.md` files gained their lines.

**C. `2d9663cc3`, `coordinator` `SKILL.md`.**
- **"Quiet times", a new first bullet:** "While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions."
- **"While the curator reads turn by turn":** "Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator." This sits with the held-list rules, where the rule already stood.
- `sources.md` gained two lines. They say that the wording and the place of the held-line rule were settled by the coordinator.

## Decisions not taken
- **`coordinator` `SKILL.md:150`:** "…or after a process stop the hook's one line." This most likely points to the git-check line that I took out, so it now points to nothing. The other reading is the stop's check-in message. Either cut the clause, or name which line it means. I left it, because the task said to change nothing else.
- **`SKILL.md:115`:** "The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn." This is mostly false now that the switch is on. Either change it to "on a turn the switch misses", or leave it. I left it.
- **`SKILL.md:152`:** "Send a push notification … only for a long run's end or a hold." This conflicts with the alarm's push. Either add the model check's alarm to that sentence, or leave it. I left it.
- **`cloud-container` `SKILL.md:45`:** "how to turn it off" no longer fits. Either change it to "how it is turned off", or leave it. I left it.

## What I could not follow, and disagreements
- The task names the review's "section 6". The list is in its "Part 3. Skill sentences the batch made false". I found every sentence the task names.
- **FACTS against the task, `:189-192`:** the review says all three cases are built. F-256 agrees for rows 748 and 750. For row 749 it says a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable holds where some value meets every constraint, but such a bound is still not read at a dotted call or at a type's use. I wrote F-256's version.
- **FACTS against the task, rung W:** the record's provenance cites P-46, P-48 and P-74. F-253 itself names no POSITIONS entry, so I copied those from the record.
- **Sentence lengths:** some sentences that carry code examples or quoted messages are over 25 words.

---
name: cloud-container
description: "How the cloud platform this repository is worked on behaves, apart from Claude Code and the repository: the machine (4 CPUs, about 15 GB of memory, no swap, timings that differ between sessions), the disk allowance and why df misleads, a disk full with no space left on device and what to delete, the network proxy and its blocked hosts (web.archive.org, labs.oracle.com), the platform's stop of the session's process about every 13 hours, idle stops and VM restarts, a VM restart that rolls the disk back, the weekly usage limit stopping a run, send_later check-ins that keep the session busy across a stop, the transcript backup and its blind spots, reading another session's transcript, the platform's git-check Stop hook, and a lost container: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, recovering the work. Load it when the disk fills or df looks wrong, when a host cannot be reached, after the session's process was stopped or the VM restarted, when commits are missing after a restart, before arming check-ins for a long wait, when the backup fails to push, and when a container is lost or a session must go on in another."
---

# The cloud container

**container**
: Virtual machine with its own disk, on which a cloud session of Claude Code runs. It holds a clone of the branch that the session was created from.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**main session**
: Top-level session of a container, which the curator talks to. The agents that it launches are not main sessions.

**coordinating session**
: Main session that keeps the project's files under `explorations/coordinator/` and launches the workers.

**process stop**
: End of the session's Claude Code process, by the platform's cap, by idleness or by a VM restart. The platform starts the process again in the same session.

**VM restart**
: Restart of the container's machine under a live session.

**check-in**
: One-shot reminder, armed with `send_later`, that wakes the main session with a message at a set time.

**Stop hook**
: Command that Claude Code runs at the end of every turn of the main session.

The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle. It can restart the VM, sometimes with the disk rolled back, and it can lose the container. Running agents survive none of these.

## Rules for every agent

- Before a long run, read the room left on the disk as `references/machine.md` says.
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook asks the main session to commit and push. Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

## The parts

- `references/machine.md`, for every agent: the machine, timings across sessions, agents at once, the disk allowance and a full disk, the blocked hosts.
- `references/stops.md`, for every agent: the kinds of process stop and their signs, a disk rolled back, the weekly usage limit, what a stop keeps here. Its section on check-ins is for the coordinating session.
- `references/hooks.md`, for the coordinating session: the transcript backup and its blind spots, the git-check hook and how to turn it off.
- `references/container-loss.md`, for the coordinating session: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, reading another session's transcript, recovering the work.

How a Claude Code session behaves anywhere (the Bash tool, long commands, waits and the prompt cache, interrupts, the automatic permission check) is `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. Running agents and resuming a run are the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

# Task: the cold read's flags on the hooks and the two rules, ruled

A cold read of `coordinator`'s `SKILL.md` and `cloud-container`'s `SKILL.md`, `hooks.md` and `stops.md`, from `c3e2b8e1f` to `3c8b6d5e7`, gave 21 flags. The coordinator's rulings follow. Make each edit as ruled, in the part named, as the skill's other rules are written.

## `coordinator` `SKILL.md`

- **C1, line 115.** Take the cold read's text: "The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part)."
- **C2, line 115.** Replace "So the hook asks for a commit only on a turn that the switch misses" with: if a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn. Answer it as line 151 says.
- **C3, line 149.** Define "away": the curator has said that he is away or asleep, or the turn started from a check-in or a hook, not from his message.
- **C4, line 149 against line 102.** While he is away, a skill change's report waits until he is back, as one message.
- **C5, lines 151 and 211.** The model check's alarm holds over the quiet times' rules, the "." reply at a check-in included.
- **C6.** Add two glossary entries in the glossary's form:
  - **model check**: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.
  - **git-check switch**: hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.
- **C7 and C8, line 199, step 0.** If either field names a model other than Opus or Fable, act as on the model check's alarm.
- **C9, line 211.** Say what the alarm is. The Stop hook makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of the reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on; if it is not, act as on the alarm.
- **C10, line 211, and `references/delegating.md` where it treats headless sessions.** The model check runs in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless ones included. A headless session started on a tier other than Opus or Fable sets `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment, or the check halts it. Today only the baseline interview does so.
- **C11, line 211.** The work stops until `get_session` shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of the reply, and send no further push notification for it.
- **Line 151, against `hooks.md:29` (H8).** The coordinating session answers a git-check reminder as line 151 says. `hooks.md` points to that line instead of giving its own rule.

## `cloud-container`

- **K1, `SKILL.md:39`.** Take the cold read's text: "The platform's git-check Stop hook can still ask the main session to commit and push on a turn that the git-check switch misses (`references/hooks.md`)."
- **H1, `hooks.md:3`.** Take the cold read's text: "The tracked `.claude/settings.json` runs three Stop hooks: the transcript backup, the `coordinator` skill's model check and the git-check switch. The launcher adds the git-check hook."
- **H2, `hooks.md:31`.** Write "the repository's `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`" and "the tracked `.claude/settings.json`".
- **H3, `hooks.md:31`.** "It replaces the script's body with two commands that read the input and exit 0".
- **H4, `hooks.md:31`.** Delete "So the hook needs no step by hand and no manual approval."
- **H5, `hooks.md:31`.** Say that the switch runs at every turn's end, so copying the `.orig` file back is undone at the next one. Turning the hook back on is the curator's decision. Give no steps for it.
- **H6, `hooks.md:33`.** Take the cold read's text: "After a git-check reminder, run `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`. If it prints 1 or more, run `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh </dev/null`."
- **H7, `hooks.md:34`.** Take the cold read's text: "Claude Code runs the Stop hooks at the same time, so on a turn after a start the git check can run before the switch empties it."
- **H8, `hooks.md:29` and `:34`.** As under line 151 above.
- **S1, `stops.md:51`.** Take the cold read's text: "Each start writes the platform's git-check script again, and the repository's `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh` turns it off again (`hooks.md`)."

## Checks and report

Add the lines for these edits to the skills' `sources.md`, each "settled by the coordinator, 2026-10-19". Keep each part no longer than it needs to be. Run the lint, commit on `main`, and push nothing.

# The transcript backup and the git-check hook

This part is for the coordinating session. Two Stop hooks run in this container.

## The transcript backup

The backup's Stop hook runs `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh`. The hook returns at once, and a detached runner does the work. It copies the transcripts of every session in the container, Workflow agents' included, into that worktree of the orphan branch `transcripts-blinded`. Then it commits, pushes and packs. A pass takes about 10 s and writes one line to the worktree's `.backup.log`, which keeps the last 200.

The tracked `.claude/settings.json` registers the hook, beside the compaction hook. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` adds it to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if the tracked file does not. If both files register it, each turn's end runs two passes, about 4 s apart, which the backup's lock runs one after the other. They do no harm.

Its blind spots:

- It runs when a turn of the main session ends, not when an agent finishes. A session inside one long turn is not backed up, however much its agents do. Check-ins end turns (`stops.md`).
- It copies transcripts, not trees. Uncommitted work in a worktree is not covered.
- If the container dies within about 10 s of a turn's end, that turn's snapshot is lost.
- It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push is silent. At each check-in and after each process stop, read the log's last line, or the branch's state. A good pass reads `push=ok`, or `ahead=0 push=none`.

      tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log
      git -C /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded status -sb

- The runner removes only an `index.lock` that is at least 10 s old and that no process holds open. A stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed` in the log). If no process holds it open, remove it by hand.

The scripts that run are the copies in the worktree's `scripts/`. The reference copies in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` change nothing until you copy them into the worktree. If a pass fails in a way that this section does not name, print `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md#Three traps'`, and the same for "How the snapshot works".

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). It exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, when the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed commits. When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

Every start of the process writes the launcher's script again. The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, then turns the hook off: `.claude/settings.json` runs it at every SessionStart and every Stop. It gives the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0, and keeps the launcher's script as `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`. So the hook needs no step by hand and no manual approval.

- To tell whether the hook is on, run `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`. It prints 1 or more while the hook is on.
- The switch can miss one turn, where its Stop run comes beside the git check itself. Answer that turn's reminder as the paragraph above says.
====
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook asks the main session to commit and push. Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 270 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

A worker whose task touches the repository loads `fortress-repo` by itself. That skill tells it which choices are its own.

## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).

## Interrupts and process stops

An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.

- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines. `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md` has such a wrapper (`resumeOrder`).
- If a batch's commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in `/home/user/fortress`. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
- If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, `git stash` its staged changes and keep the stash before you resume.
- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript: the safety filter can end a Fable worker that prints one.

# Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers

**Workflow run**
: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.

**journal**
: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call and a `result` line with its structured result.

**headless session**
: `claude -p` session started from your shell.

**archaeology**
: Search of git and the transcripts for how something came about. It returns cited evidence, not a judgement.

## Which tier runs what

- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
- Use Sonnet for archaeology and retrieval only, never for a judgement.
- When this session runs on Fable, have an Opus worker write each longer report or page for the curator.
- Take a cross-area question in two steps. First, Opus workers gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.

## What a brief holds

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
- The entries that it needs, quoted word for word under their numbers. Quote a rule of the curator's whole, with its limit and its example.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 270 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

A worker whose task touches the repository loads `fortress-repo` by itself. That skill tells it which choices are its own.

## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).

## Interrupts and process stops

An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.

- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines. `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md` has such a wrapper (`resumeOrder`).
- If a batch's commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in `/home/user/fortress`. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
- If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, `git stash` its staged changes and keep the stash before you resume.
- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript: the safety filter can end a Fable worker that prints one.

## The Workflow tool

- The tool runs at most two agents at once on this machine. The others wait.
- Across agents, the cache serves the first message only when the whole prompt is identical. A project agent type's system prompt is cached for every agent of the type, so put text that every agent needs there.
- A project agent type written during the session is found only after a process stop. A project skill appears at once.
- `agent()` can return null for an agent that the harness marks failed after it delivered its result. Read its branch before you run it again.
- Check a script by parsing it as an async function body, not with `node --check`: `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js`.

## A second session

A second coordinating session contributes reviews and their commits, on a branch of its own from `main`. It runs no batch and does not change PLAN's order.

name: cloud-container
description: "How the cloud platform this repository is worked on behaves, apart from Claude Code and the repository: the machine (4 CPUs, about 15 GB of memory, no swap, timings that differ between sessions), the disk allowance and why df misleads, a disk full with no space left on device and what to delete, the network proxy and its blocked hosts (web.archive.org, labs.oracle.com), the platform's stop of the session's process about every 13 hours, idle stops and VM restarts, a VM restart that rolls the disk back, the weekly usage limit stopping a run, send_later check-ins that keep the session busy across a stop, the transcript backup and its blind spots, reading another session's transcript, the platform's git-check Stop hook, and a lost container: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, recovering the work. Load it when the disk fills or df looks wrong, when a host cannot be reached, after the session's process was stopped or the VM restarted, when commits are missing after a restart, before arming check-ins for a long wait, when the backup fails to push, and when a container is lost or a session must go on in another."

# The cloud container

**container**
: Virtual machine with its own disk, on which a cloud session of Claude Code runs. It holds a clone of the branch that the session was created from.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**main session**
: Top-level session of a container, which the curator talks to. The agents that it launches are not main sessions.

**coordinating session**
: Main session that keeps the project's files under `explorations/coordinator/` and launches the workers.

**process stop**
: End of the session's Claude Code process, by the platform's cap, by idleness or by a VM restart. The platform starts the process again in the same session.

**VM restart**
: Restart of the container's machine under a live session.

**check-in**
: One-shot reminder, armed with `send_later`, that wakes the main session with a message at a set time.

**Stop hook**
: Command that Claude Code runs at the end of every turn of the main session.

The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle. It can restart the VM, sometimes with the disk rolled back, and it can lose the container. Running agents survive none of these.

## Rules for every agent

- Before a long run, read the room left on the disk as `references/machine.md` says.
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook asks the main session to commit and push. Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

## The parts

- `references/machine.md`, for every agent: the machine, timings across sessions, agents at once, the disk allowance and a full disk, the blocked hosts.
- `references/stops.md`, for every agent: the kinds of process stop and their signs, a disk rolled back, the weekly usage limit, what a stop keeps here. Its section on check-ins is for the coordinating session.
- `references/hooks.md`, for the coordinating session: the transcript backup and its blind spots, the git-check hook and how it is turned off.
- `references/container-loss.md`, for the coordinating session: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, reading another session's transcript, recovering the work.

How a Claude Code session behaves anywhere (the Bash tool, long commands, waits and the prompt cache, interrupts, the automatic permission check) is `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. Running agents and resuming a run are the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

# The transcript backup and the git-check hook

This part is for the coordinating session. Two Stop hooks run in this container.

## The transcript backup

The backup's Stop hook runs `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh`. The hook returns at once, and a detached runner does the work. It copies the transcripts of every session in the container, Workflow agents' included, into that worktree of the orphan branch `transcripts-blinded`. Then it commits, pushes and packs. A pass takes about 10 s and writes one line to the worktree's `.backup.log`, which keeps the last 200.

The tracked `.claude/settings.json` registers the hook, beside the compaction hook. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` adds it to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if the tracked file does not. If both files register it, each turn's end runs two passes, about 4 s apart, which the backup's lock runs one after the other. They do no harm.

Its blind spots:

- It runs when a turn of the main session ends, not when an agent finishes. A session inside one long turn is not backed up, however much its agents do. Check-ins end turns (`stops.md`).
- It copies transcripts, not trees. Uncommitted work in a worktree is not covered.
- If the container dies within about 10 s of a turn's end, that turn's snapshot is lost.
- It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push is silent. At each check-in and after each process stop, read the log's last line, or the branch's state. A good pass reads `push=ok`, or `ahead=0 push=none`.

      tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log
      git -C /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded status -sb

- The runner removes only an `index.lock` that is at least 10 s old and that no process holds open. A stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed` in the log). If no process holds it open, remove it by hand.

The scripts that run are the copies in the worktree's `scripts/`. The reference copies in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` change nothing until you copy them into the worktree. If a pass fails in a way that this section does not name, print `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md#Three traps'`, and the same for "How the snapshot works".

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). It exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, when the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed commits. When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

Every start of the process writes the launcher's script again. The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, then turns the hook off: `.claude/settings.json` runs it at every SessionStart and every Stop. It gives the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0, and keeps the launcher's script as `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`. So the hook needs no step by hand and no manual approval.

- To tell whether the hook is on, run `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`. It prints 1 or more while the hook is on.
- The switch can miss one turn, where its Stop run comes beside the git check itself. Answer that turn's reminder as the paragraph above says.

# The transcript backup and the git-check hook

This part is for the coordinating session. The tracked `.claude/settings.json` runs three Stop hooks: the transcript backup, the `coordinator` skill's model check and the git-check switch. The launcher adds the git-check hook.

## The transcript backup

The backup's Stop hook runs `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh`. The hook returns at once, and a detached runner does the work. It copies the transcripts of every session in the container, Workflow agents' included, into that worktree of the orphan branch `transcripts-blinded`. Then it commits, pushes and packs. A pass takes about 10 s and writes one line to the worktree's `.backup.log`, which keeps the last 200.

The tracked `.claude/settings.json` registers the hook, beside the compaction hook. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` adds it to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if the tracked file does not. If both files register it, each turn's end runs two passes, about 4 s apart, which the backup's lock runs one after the other. They do no harm.

Its blind spots:

- It runs when a turn of the main session ends, not when an agent finishes. A session inside one long turn is not backed up, however much its agents do. Check-ins end turns (`stops.md`).
- It copies transcripts, not trees. Uncommitted work in a worktree is not covered.
- If the container dies within about 10 s of a turn's end, that turn's snapshot is lost.
- It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push is silent. At each check-in and after each process stop, read the log's last line, or the branch's state. A good pass reads `push=ok`, or `ahead=0 push=none`.

      tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log
      git -C /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded status -sb

- The runner removes only an `index.lock` that is at least 10 s old and that no process holds open. A stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed` in the log). If no process holds it open, remove it by hand.

The scripts that run are the copies in the worktree's `scripts/`. The reference copies in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` change nothing until you copy them into the worktree. If a pass fails in a way that this section does not name, print `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md#Three traps'`, and the same for "How the snapshot works".

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). It exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, when the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed commits. When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

Every start of the process writes the launcher's script again. The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, then turns the hook off: `.claude/settings.json` runs it at every SessionStart and every Stop. It gives the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0, and keeps the launcher's script as `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`. So the hook needs no step by hand and no manual approval.

- To tell whether the hook is on, run `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`. It prints 1 or more while the hook is on.
- The switch can miss one turn, where its Stop run comes beside the git check itself. Answer that turn's reminder as the paragraph above says.

# The platform's stops, and check-ins

This part says when the platform's stops come, how to tell them apart, and what they do here. What any process stop kills and keeps, and a worker's steps after one, are `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. How to resume a run is the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

## What stops the process

- **The cap.** The platform stops the process after about 12 h 58 min of continuous running, and starts it again in resume mode, the same session, within seconds. No crash, memory limit or message causes it. The next stop comes 12 h 58 min after the last start.
- **Idleness.** The process also ends when the session goes idle, after a few minutes to a few hours. It runs continuously only while the curator or a check-in keeps it busy, so the cap's stops fall in busy stretches.
- **A VM restart.** The machine boots again. The disk usually survives (below).

Every start, after a VM restart too, resets the cap's clock.

The environment manager's log records every stop and start:

    grep -E 'Received signal|context cancellation|Set session mode' /tmp/env-manager.log | tail

A stop is three lines: a `SIGTERM` ("Received signal, shutting down gracefully"), then "Claude Code stopped due to context cancellation" with the run's length in `duration_ms`, then "Set session mode for environment" `resume`, the next start. To tell the kinds apart:

- The cap's stop has a `duration_ms` near 46,640,000.
- An idle stop has a shorter one, and the boot time that `uptime -s` prints stays earlier than the stop.
- After a VM restart, `uptime -s` prints a boot time between the stop and the next start.

## A VM restart that rolls the disk back

A VM restart can bring the disk back to an earlier state. Other restarts have kept it whole, and nothing tells in advance which kind comes. So only what is pushed is safe.

The signs of a rollback:

- The local `main` ends at an earlier commit, and the commits made since are on `origin` only. The reflog jumps from that commit to the first commit made after the restart.
- The newer files of the scratchpad and of the tree's `tmp/` are gone, and so are the later lines of the backup's log. The session's own transcript stays whole.

To recover:

1. Run `git fetch`.
2. On each branch that you work on, `main` included, run `git rebase origin/<branch>`. With no commit after the restart, this moves the branch forward to the pushed commit.
3. Push your own commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says.
4. In the coordinating session, after the next turn ends, read the backup's last log line (`hooks.md`).

If the source file of a published Artifact page was lost, the `coordinator` skill says how to rebuild it from the page.

## The weekly usage limit

When the account's weekly limit on all models is reached, each new agent launch is refused ("You've hit your weekly limit"), and a running Workflow run ends. Later, turns and launches can be served again while the usage panel still shows the limit as reached. A launch that succeeds is the sign. If the limit ended a run, resume it as after a process stop.

## What a stop kills and keeps here

Any process stop kills and keeps what `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md` says. On this platform, also:

- `send_later` reminders survive. They live on the server.
- A command started with `nohup` survives the cap and an idle stop. A VM restart ends every process.
- The launcher writes the git-check hook again, and the git-check switch turns it off at the start (`hooks.md`).

A new session is not a process stop. It starts on a fresh machine and cannot resume another session's run. Only its pushed work and the files of the repository carry over.

## Check-ins, for the coordinating session

Check-ins keep the session busy across a long run. Each wake falls inside the main session's one-hour prompt cache, so it reads the cache instead of writing the whole context again. Each turn's end also runs the transcript backup (`hooks.md`).

- Arm all the check-ins of a series in one turn, 45 minutes apart. Use no cron trigger, whose shortest interval is an hour. Do not chain reminders, each check-in arming the next one.
- The scheduler refuses more than about ten trigger creations a minute ("Trigger creation rate limit reached"). If it refuses one, arm the rest a minute later.
- A series ends with its last check-in. If the run outlasts it, have the last check-in arm a whole new series.
- Add one check-in a few minutes after the cap's next stop, 12 h 58 min after the last start. In its message, tell the session to resume what the stop killed.
- After a stop, or when you relaunch a run, delete or re-arm the reminders to fit the run.
- An interrupt of any turn, one that a check-in started included, kills the run's agents. If the curator means to stop the session while agents run, ask them to wait until the turn has ended and about 10 s more, for the backup's pass.
